section.heading: 12.6. Cylinders and Quadric Surfaces
section.paragraph: We have already looked at two special types of surfaces: planes (in Section 12.5) and spheres (in Section 12.1). Here we investigate two other types of surfaces: cylinders and quadric surfaces.

In order to sketch the graph of a surface, it is useful to determine the curves of intersection of the surface with planes parallel to the coordinate planes. These curves are called traces (or cross-sections) of the surface.
section.heading: Cylinders
section.paragraph: A cylinder is a surface that consists of all lines (called rulings) that are parallel to a given line and pass through a given plane curve.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the surface $$z = x^{2}$$ .

Solution Notice that the equation of the graph, $$z = x^{2}$$ , doesn’t involve $$y$$ . This means that any vertical plane with equation $$y = k$$ (parallel to the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane) intersects the graph in a curve with equation $$z = x^{2}$$ . So these vertical traces are parabolas. Figure 1 shows how the graph is formed by taking the parabola $$z = x^{2}$$ in the $$\mathit{xz}$$ -plane and moving it in the direction of the $$y$$ -axis. The graph is a surface, called a parabolic cylinder, made up of infinitely many shifted copies of the same parabola. Here the rulings of the cylinder are parallel to the $$y$$ -axis.

image.alt: Details A rectangular sheet is graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The sheet is bent such that the curved sides trace a parabola opening upwards, parallel to the x z plane. The bottom-most part of the sheet falls on the y axis. At approximately the middle of the rectangular sheet, the parabolic curve created by the bend is outlined such that it is symmetric about the z axis with its vertex at the origin. Equidistant horizontal lines are drawn on the outer surface of the sheet, parallel to the x y plane.

figure.caption: The surface $$z = x^{2}$$ is a parabolic cylinder.

section.paragraph: In Example 1 the variable $$y$$ is missing from the equation of the cylinder. This is typical of a surface whose rulings are parallel to one of the coordinate axes. If one of the variables $$x$$ , $$y$$ , or $$z$$ is missing from the equation of a surface, then the surface is a cylinder.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Identify and sketch the surfaces.
Solution

(See Figure 2. We first encountered this surface in Example 12.1.2.) Here the rulings are vertical lines. (b) In this case $$x$$ is missing and the surface is a circular cylinder whose axis is the $$x$$ -axis. (See Figure 3.) It is obtained by taking the circle $$y^{2} + z^{2} = 1$$ , $$x = 0$$ in the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane and moving it parallel to the $$x$$ -axis. section.paragraph: Note When you are dealing with surfaces, it is important to recognize that an equation like $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ represents a cylinder and not a circle. The trace of the cylinder $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is the circle with equations $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 1$$ , $$z = 0$$ .
section.heading: Quadric Surfaces
section.paragraph: A quadric surface is the graph of a second-degree equation in three variables $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ . The most general such equation is
$$Ax^{2} + By^{2} + Cz^{2} + Dxy + Eyz + Fxz + Gx + Hy + Iz + J = 0$$
where $$A,B,C,\ldots,J$$ are constants, but by translation and rotation it can be brought into one of the two standard forms
Quadric surfaces are the counterparts in three dimensions of the conic sections in the plane. (See Section 10.5 for a review of conic sections.)

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Use traces to sketch the quadric surface with equation

Solution By substituting $$z = 0$$ , we find that the trace in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane is $$x^{2} + y^{2} \slash 9 = 1$$ , which we recognize as an equation of an ellipse. In general, the horizontal trace in the plane $$z = k$$ is

which is an ellipse, provided that $$k^{2} < 4$$ , that is, $$- 2 < k < 2$$ . (If $$\left| k \middle| = 2 \right.$$ , the trace consists of a single point, and the trace is empty for $$\left| k \middle| > 2 \right.$$ .)
Similarly, vertical traces parallel to the $$\mathit{yz}$$ - and $$\mathit{xz}$$ -planes are also ellipses:

Figure 4 shows how drawing some traces indicates the shape of the surface. It’s called an ellipsoid because all of its traces are ellipses. Notice that it is symmetric with respect to each coordinate plane; this is because its equation involves only even powers of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ .

image.alt: Details An ellipsoid and four ellipses are graphed in the x y z coordinate plane. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The length of the ellipsoid is along the y axis and its width is along the x axis. The outer surface of the ellipsoid crosses the x, y, and z axes at (1, 0, 0), (0, 3, 0), and (0, 0, 2), respectively. Four ellipses are outlined on the outer surface of the ellipsoid. The third ellipse lies on the x z plane, with its center at the origin and passing through (1, 0, 0) and (0, 0, 2) on the x and z axes, respectively. The fourth ellipse is parallel to the third one, with its center at the positive y axis.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Use traces to sketch the surface $$z = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ .

Solution If we put $$x = 0$$ , we get $$z = y^{2}$$ , so the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane intersects the surface in a parabola. If we put $$x = k$$ (a constant), we get $$z = y^{2} + 4k^{2}$$ . This means that if we slice the graph with any plane parallel to the $$\mathit{yz}$$ -plane, we obtain a parabola that opens upward. Similarly, if $$y = k$$ , the trace is $$z = 4x^{2} + k^{2}$$ , which is again a parabola that opens upward. If we put $$z = k$$ , we get the horizontal traces $$4x^{2} + y^{2} = k$$ , which we recognize as a family of ellipses $$(k > 0)$$ . Knowing the shapes of the traces, we can sketch the graph in Figure 5. Because of the elliptical and parabolic traces, the quadric surface $$z = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is called an elliptic paraboloid.

image.alt: Details An elliptic paraboloid, three parabolas, and an ellipse are graphed in the x y z coordinate space. The positive x axis slopes down and to the left. The positive y axis slopes slightly down and to the right. The positive z axis runs vertically upward. The elliptic paraboloid has its vertex at the origin, opens upward, and resembles a paraboloid with its sides flattened such that horizontal cross-sections of the paraboloid are ellipses. The x z plane cuts the elliptic paraboloid such that the outer surface of the paraboloid traces a parabola opening upward with its vertex at the origin and symmetric about the positive z axis. The y z plane cuts the elliptic paraboloid such that the outer surface of the paraboloid traces a parabola opening upward with its vertex at the origin and symmetric about the positive z axis. A vertical trace at the top right of the elliptic paraboloid is shaped like a parabola. A horizontal trace of the paraboloid, parallel to the x y plane is in the shape of an ellipse centered on the positive z axis.

figure.caption: The surface $$z = 4x^{2} + y^{2}$$ is an elliptic paraboloid. Horizontal traces are ellipses; vertical traces are parabolas.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Sketch the surface $$z = y^{2} - x^{2}$$ .

Solution The traces in the vertical planes $$x = k$$ are the parabolas $$z = y^{2} - k^{2}$$ , which open upward. The traces in $$y = k$$ are the parabolas $$z = - x^{2} + k^{2}$$ , which open downward. The horizontal traces are $$y^{2} - x^{2} = k$$ , a family of hyperbolas. We draw the families of traces in Figure 6, and we show how the traces appear when placed in their correct planes in Figure 7.

Notice that the shape of the surface near the origin resembles that of a saddle. This surface will be investigated further in Section 14.7 when we discuss saddle points.

section.paragraph: The idea of using traces to draw a surface is employed in three-dimensional graphing software. In most such software, traces in the vertical planes $$x = k$$ and $$y = k$$ are drawn for equally spaced values of $$k$$ . Table 1 shows computer-drawn graphs of the six basic types of quadric surfaces in standard form. All surfaces are symmetric with respect to the $$z$$ -axis. If a quadric surface is symmetric about a different axis, its equation changes accordingly.
section.heading: Table 1 Graphs of Quadric Surfaces

row.cell: $$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}} = 1$$ All traces are ellipses. If $$a = b = c$$ , the ellipsoid is a sphere.
$$\frac{z}{c} = \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}$$ Horizontal traces are ellipses. Vertical traces are parabolas. The variable raised to the first power indicates the axis of the paraboloid.
$$\frac{z}{c} = \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}$$ Horizontal traces are hyperbolas. Vertical traces are parabolas. The case where $$c < 0$$ is illustrated.

$$\frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}} = \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}$$ Horizontal traces are ellipses. Vertical traces in the planes $$x = k$$ and $$y = k$$ are hyperbolas if $$k \neq 0$$ but are pairs of lines if $$k = 0$$ .

$$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} - \frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}} = 1$$ Horizontal traces are ellipses. Vertical traces are hyperbolas. The axis of symmetry corresponds to the variable whose coefficient is negative.

$$- \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} + \frac{z^{2}}{c^{2}} = 1$$ Horizontal traces in $$z = k$$ are ellipses if $$k > c$$ or $$k < - c$$ . Vertical traces are hyperbolas. The two minus signs indicate two sheets.

section.heading: Applications of Quadric Surfaces
section.paragraph: Examples of quadric surfaces can be found in the world around us. In fact, the world itself is a good example. Although the earth is commonly modeled as a sphere, a more accurate model is an ellipsoid because the earth’s rotation has caused a flattening at the poles. (See Exercise 51.)

Circular paraboloids, obtained by rotating a parabola about its axis, are used to collect and reflect light, sound, and radio and television signals [see Figure 12(a)]. In a radio telescope, for instance, signals from distant stars that strike the bowl are all reflected to the receiver at the focus and are therefore amplified. (The idea is explained in Problem 22 in the Problems Plus following Chapter 3.) The same principle applies to microphones and satellite dishes in the shape of paraboloids.

image.alt: Details A photograph of a satellite dish. A photograph of two cooling towers of nuclear reactors. A photograph of gears in the shape of hyperboloids.

section.paragraph: Cooling towers for nuclear reactors are usually designed in the shape of hyperboloids of one sheet [Figure 12(b)] for reasons of structural stability. Pairs of hyperboloids are used to transmit rotational motion between skew axes. [See Figure 12(c); the cogs of the gears are the generating lines of the hyperboloids. See Exercise 53.]
